title.en: Section 1 - Conversation at a Museum Information Desk
title.zh: 第一部分 - 博物馆咨询台的对话

sections.passage:
A visitor approaches the information desk at the National History Museum to inquire about membership options and upcoming exhibitions. The receptionist, Helen, greets the visitor and asks how she can help. The visitor explains that he recently moved to the area and is interested in becoming a regular visitor to the museum. Helen explains that the museum offers several membership tiers. The standard individual membership costs 45 pounds per year and includes unlimited free entry to all permanent galleries, a 10 percent discount at the museum shop, and a quarterly newsletter. The premium membership at 75 pounds per year adds priority booking for special exhibitions, invitations to members-only evening events, and free audio guides. There is also a family membership for 120 pounds that covers two adults and up to three children under 16.

The visitor asks about the current special exhibition on ancient Egyptian artifacts. Helen tells him it runs from March 15th through June 30th and features over 300 objects loaned from museums in Cairo, including items from the tomb of Tutankhamun that have never been displayed outside Egypt before. Standard admission to the special exhibition is 12 pounds for adults, but members receive a 50 percent discount. The visitor also inquires about the museum's opening hours. Helen explains that the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 AM to 5:30 PM, with extended hours until 8 PM on Fridays. The museum is closed on Mondays except during school holidays. Parking is available in the adjacent multi-story car park at a flat rate of 5 pounds per visit for museum visitors, which can be validated at the reception desk.

title.en: Section 2 - Guided Tour of a Wildlife Park
title.zh: 第二部分 - 野生动物园导览

sections.passage:
Welcome to Thornfield Wildlife Park, one of the region's leading conservation centers. My name is James, and I'll be your guide for today's visit. Before we begin, I'd like to give you some important information about the park and its facilities.

The park covers 85 hectares of mixed woodland and open grassland, and is home to over 400 animals representing 85 different species. We are particularly proud of our breeding programs for endangered species, including the red panda, the snow leopard, and the African wild dog. Our most recent success has been the birth of two snow leopard cubs in January, which brings our total to six snow leopards here at the park.

Today's tour will take approximately two hours and covers a distance of about three kilometers. We'll start at the Education Center, where you can see our reptile collection and learn about local conservation efforts. From there, we'll walk through the woodland trail to the bird of prey arena, where we have a flying demonstration at 11:30 AM and again at 2:30 PM. After that, we'll visit the big cat enclosures and finish at the primate house.

I should mention that the park has two cafes. The Woodland Cafe is located near the main entrance and serves hot meals and snacks from 9 AM to 4 PM. The Lakeside Cafe, which is near the primate house, offers lighter refreshments and is open from 10 AM to 3:30 PM. We also have a gift shop near the exit, which stocks a range of educational toys, books, and souvenirs. All proceeds from the gift shop go directly to our conservation projects.

For safety reasons, please do not attempt to feed any of the animals. Flash photography is prohibited in the reptile house and the nocturnal animal section, as it can distress the animals. If you have any questions during the tour, please feel free to ask. We want you to have an enjoyable and educational experience.

title.en: Section 3 - Discussion Between Two Students About a Research Project
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生关于研究项目的讨论

sections.passage:
Sarah and Tom are final-year psychology students discussing their joint research project on the effects of social media usage on sleep quality among university students. They meet in the library to review their progress and plan the next phase of their research.

Sarah begins by summarizing their literature review findings. She has identified several key studies that demonstrate a correlation between excessive social media use and poor sleep outcomes. One particularly relevant study by Dr. Martinez at the University of Melbourne found that students who spent more than three hours per day on social media platforms reported significantly higher rates of insomnia and daytime fatigue. However, Sarah notes that most existing studies rely on self-reported data, which may not be entirely reliable.

Tom suggests that they should incorporate both quantitative and qualitative methods in their research. For the quantitative component, they plan to distribute an online survey to 200 undergraduate students across three faculties: Arts, Science, and Business. The survey will include standardized questionnaires measuring social media addiction, sleep quality using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and general wellbeing. For the qualitative component, they intend to conduct semi-structured interviews with 20 selected participants who represent a range of social media usage patterns.

They discuss the ethical considerations of their study. Since they are collecting sensitive data about mental health and personal habits, they need to ensure full anonymity and obtain ethics approval from the university's Research Ethics Committee. Sarah mentions that their supervisor, Professor Williams, has already reviewed their ethics application and suggested some minor amendments, particularly regarding the informed consent form and data storage procedures. They need to use encrypted storage for all participant data and destroy raw data within twelve months of the project's completion.

Regarding the timeline, they agree that data collection should be completed by mid-March, allowing two months for analysis and write-up before the May deadline. Tom will handle the statistical analysis using SPSS software, while Sarah will code the interview transcripts using thematic analysis. They plan to meet weekly to discuss their findings and ensure consistency between the two data sets.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on Sustainable Urban Development
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于可持续城市发展的讲座

sections.passage:
Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is the third in our series on sustainable urban development, and I'll be focusing on the concept of green infrastructure and its role in creating livable cities for the future.

Green infrastructure refers to the network of natural and semi-natural areas, green spaces, and other environmental features within and around urban areas. Unlike traditional grey infrastructure, which relies on engineered solutions such as concrete drainage systems, green infrastructure uses natural processes to manage water, reduce pollution, and improve air quality. Examples include urban forests, green roofs, rain gardens, permeable pavements, and constructed wetlands.

Let me give you some concrete examples of successful green infrastructure projects. Singapore is widely regarded as a global leader in this field. The city-state's Gardens by the Bay project, completed in 2012, transformed 101 hectares of reclaimed land into a spectacular nature park featuring solar-powered supertrees, cloud forests, and extensive biodiversity gardens. The project has reduced ambient temperatures in the surrounding area by up to 4 degrees Celsius and attracts over 9 million visitors annually.

Copenhagen provides another excellent example. The city has invested heavily in cycling infrastructure and now has over 400 kilometers of dedicated cycle lanes. As a result, 62 percent of residents commute to work or school by bicycle, making it one of the most cycling-friendly cities in the world. This has led to a 30 percent reduction in carbon emissions from the transport sector since 2005. Additionally, Copenhagen has implemented a cloudburst management plan that uses green infrastructure to handle extreme rainfall events, which are becoming more frequent due to climate change.

Here in the UK, the city of Sheffield has undertaken an ambitious urban tree planting program, planting over 500,000 trees since 2015. Research conducted by the University of Sheffield has shown that these trees remove approximately 200 tonnes of air pollutants annually and provide a cooling effect equivalent to saving 2.5 million pounds in air conditioning costs. The program has also created over 200 green jobs and significantly increased property values in previously deprived neighborhoods.

However, implementing green infrastructure is not without challenges. Initial costs can be significantly higher than conventional approaches, and the benefits often take years or decades to fully materialize. There are also issues of maintenance, as green infrastructure requires ongoing care and management. Furthermore, there can be conflicts between different stakeholders, particularly when green spaces compete with development land in densely populated areas. Despite these challenges, the evidence overwhelmingly supports the long-term economic, environmental, and social benefits of investing in green infrastructure.

title.zh: 文章1 - 澳大利亚的体育成就

sections.passage:
In the world of international sport, few countries can match the per capita success of Australia. With a population of just 23 million, Australia consistently ranks among the top medal-winning nations at the Olympic Games and performs exceptionally well across a wide range of sports including swimming, cricket, rugby, tennis, and cycling. What accounts for this remarkable sporting achievement?

Several factors contribute to Australia's sporting prowess. First, the country's climate and geography naturally encourage outdoor physical activity. With vast coastlines, warm temperatures for much of the year, and abundant open spaces, Australians grow up with opportunities to participate in sport from an early age. Swimming, surfing, and beach culture are deeply embedded in the national identity, and many of the country's Olympic champions began competitive swimming before the age of ten.

Second, Australia has developed a sophisticated system of sports funding and governance. The Australian Institute of Sport (AIS), established in 1981 in Canberra, has been instrumental in identifying and developing elite athletes. The AIS provides world-class coaching, sports science support, medical services, and training facilities across more than 35 sports. Athletes selected for AIS programs receive scholarships that cover living expenses, allowing them to train full-time without financial hardship. The institute's systematic approach to talent identification, involving nationwide testing programs in schools, has been particularly effective in sports such as swimming, rowing, and track cycling.

Third, Australia benefits from a strong sporting culture that permeates all levels of society. School sport is an integral part of the education system, with most schools offering a diverse range of competitive and recreational sports. Community sporting clubs are widespread and affordable, providing pathways from grassroots participation to elite competition. The visibility of successful athletes in the media creates role models who inspire the next generation of sporting talent.

However, Australia's sporting success is not without controversy. Critics point to the uneven distribution of funding, with so-called glamour sports such as swimming and athletics receiving disproportionate resources compared to less popular sports. There have also been concerns about the pressure placed on young athletes, with some arguing that the talent identification system can be overly aggressive, pushing children into intensive training regimes before they are physically or psychologically ready. Additionally, Australia has faced several doping scandals, most notably in cycling and rugby league, which have raised questions about the integrity of the country's sporting institutions.

Despite these challenges, Australia continues to punch above its weight on the international sporting stage. The country's investment in sports science research, its commitment to developing athletes from a young age, and its deep-rooted cultural love of sport ensure that it will remain a formidable force in world sport for the foreseeable future. The Australian government recently announced an additional 200 million dollars in funding for Olympic preparation ahead of the 2028 Games, signaling its continued commitment to sporting excellence.

title.zh: 文章2 - 公共交通的优势

sections.passage:
A developed nation's transport infrastructure is a key indicator of its economic progress and quality of life. Countries that invest in efficient public transportation systems reap significant benefits in terms of reduced congestion, lower pollution levels, improved public health, and enhanced social equity. Yet many developed nations remain heavily dependent on private automobiles, a trend that carries substantial economic and environmental costs.

The economic case for public transport is compelling. A single bus can carry the equivalent of 40 to 80 cars' worth of passengers, depending on occupancy rates. This means that investing in bus rapid transit systems, light rail, or subway networks can dramatically reduce the number of vehicles on the road, thereby decreasing congestion and the associated costs of lost productivity. In the United States alone, traffic congestion is estimated to cost the economy over 87 billion dollars annually in wasted time and fuel. Cities with well-developed public transport systems, such as Tokyo, Hong Kong, and Zurich, consistently demonstrate that high-quality transit can support vibrant, productive economies.

Environmental benefits are equally significant. Transportation accounts for approximately 25 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, with private vehicles being the largest single source in many countries. Public transport produces far fewer emissions per passenger kilometer than private cars. A full bus produces roughly one-tenth of the carbon dioxide per passenger compared to a single-occupancy vehicle. Electric trains and trams are even cleaner, particularly when powered by renewable electricity. Cities that have invested heavily in public transport, such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam, have achieved substantially lower per capita transport emissions than car-dependent cities of comparable size.

Public transport also promotes social equity by providing mobility to those who cannot drive or afford a car. Elderly people, young people, people with disabilities, and low-income households all depend on accessible and affordable public transit. Research consistently shows that access to reliable public transport is one of the strongest predictors of economic opportunity for disadvantaged communities. A study by the Brookings Institution found that the typical job in a major American metropolitan area is accessible by public transport from only 30 percent of the surrounding area, highlighting significant gaps in transit coverage that limit employment opportunities for many residents.

Health benefits provide another strong argument for public transport investment. Regular public transport users tend to walk more than car drivers, as they must travel to and from stops and stations. Studies have found that public transport users take an average of 19 minutes more physical activity per day than non-users, which contributes to lower rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. Furthermore, reducing the number of cars on the road improves air quality, which in turn reduces respiratory illnesses and premature deaths caused by air pollution.

Despite these well-documented advantages, public transport faces persistent challenges. Funding is often inadequate, with many systems relying on subsidies that are vulnerable to political changes. Service quality can be inconsistent, and many suburban and rural areas remain poorly served. Overcoming the cultural preference for private cars remains perhaps the greatest challenge, particularly in countries like the United States and Australia where car ownership is deeply ingrained in the national psyche. Nevertheless, growing concerns about climate change, urban congestion, and energy security are driving renewed interest in public transport investment worldwide.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Search for Anti-Aging Solutions
title.zh: 文章3 - 寻找抗衰老方案

sections.passage:
The quest to extend human lifespan has captivated scientists, philosophers, and ordinary people for centuries. In recent decades, however, advances in molecular biology and genetics have transformed the search for anti-aging interventions from speculative fiction into a legitimate area of scientific research. Today, a growing number of researchers believe that aging itself may be treatable, potentially allowing humans to live significantly longer and healthier lives.

One of the most promising areas of anti-aging research involves caloric restriction, the practice of reducing calorie intake by 20 to 40 percent below normal levels while maintaining adequate nutrition. Studies in animals ranging from yeast and worms to mice and primates have consistently shown that caloric restriction extends lifespan by 20 to 50 percent. In a landmark study conducted at the University of Wisconsin, rhesus monkeys on calorie-restricted diets showed dramatically lower rates of age-related diseases including cancer, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease compared to control groups eating normal diets. However, translating these findings to humans has proven challenging, as few people are willing or able to maintain such severe dietary restrictions over long periods.

Pharmaceutical approaches to anti-aging have shown considerable promise. Rapamycin, a drug originally developed to prevent organ transplant rejection, has been found to extend the lifespan of mice by 10 to 15 percent when administered in low doses. The drug works by inhibiting a protein called mTOR, which plays a key role in regulating cell growth and metabolism. Similarly, metformin, a widely used diabetes medication, has demonstrated anti-aging properties in laboratory studies and is now being tested in a major clinical trial called TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) involving 3,000 participants aged 65 to 79 across 14 research centers in the United States.

Perhaps the most revolutionary approach involves senolytics, a class of drugs designed to selectively eliminate senescent cells. These are cells that have stopped dividing but refuse to die, accumulating in tissues and releasing inflammatory chemicals that damage surrounding healthy cells. Researchers at the Mayo Clinic have shown that clearing senescent cells from mice extends their healthy lifespan by approximately 25 percent and reverses many age-related conditions, including cataracts, muscle weakness, and cognitive decline. Several senolytic drugs are now in early-stage human clinical trials.

Genetic research has also yielded fascinating insights into the biology of aging. Studies of centenarians, people who live to 100 or beyond, have identified several genetic variants associated with exceptional longevity, including variations in the APOE and FOXO3 genes. Meanwhile, researchers studying the telomeres, the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes that shorten with each cell division, have discovered that the enzyme telomerase can rebuild telomeres and effectively reverse cellular aging in laboratory settings. The 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to three scientists for their discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.

Critics of anti-aging research raise important ethical and social concerns. If life-extending treatments become available, they will likely be expensive and accessible only to the wealthy, potentially creating a society divided between those who can afford to live longer and those who cannot. There are also concerns about the impact on population growth, pension systems, and intergenerational equity. Some bioethicists argue that resources would be better spent on improving healthcare for existing populations rather than extending lifespan for a privileged few. Despite these concerns, investment in anti-aging research continues to grow, with private foundations and technology billionaires pouring billions of dollars into the field.

text.zh: 雷帕霉素能将小鼠的寿命延长多少？

text.zh: 雷帕霉素通过抑制什么来延长寿命？

text.zh: TAME临床试验有多少参与者？

text.en: What are senescent cells?
text.zh: 衰老细胞是什么？

options.en: Cells that have stopped dividing but refuse to die
options.zh: 停止分裂但拒绝死亡的细胞

options.en: Cells that only exist in older people
options.zh: 只存在于老年人体内的细胞

text.zh: 清除衰老细胞能将小鼠的健康寿命延长多少？

text.zh: 哪个机构在研究衰老细胞清除药物？

text.zh: 哪些基因变异与超常寿命相关？

text.zh: 细胞分裂时端粒会发生什么变化？

prompt.en: The graph below shows the consumption of fish and some different kinds of meat in a European country between 1979 and 2004. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

prompt.en: Some people think that instead of preventing climate change, we need to find a way to live with it. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为，与其防止气候变化，不如想办法适应它。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？给出你回答的理由，并包括来自你自己的知识或经验的相关例子。至少写250个单词。
